"""
A simple neural network with four inputs, two hidden layers and one output layer.
Also includes a Tkinter GUI to visualize the network’s neurons and connections.
"""

import numpy as np
import tkinter as tk

# ---------------------------
# Neural Network Definition
# ---------------------------
class NeuralNetwork:
    def __init__(self, input_size=4, hidden_sizes=[5, 3], output_size=1):
        # Layer dimensions: input, hidden layer 1, hidden layer 2, output
        self.layers = [input_size] + hidden_sizes + [output_size]
        # Initialize weights and biases for each connection between layers
        # We use a small random initialization (e.g., from a normal distribution)
        self.weights = []
        self.biases  = []
        for i in range(len(self.layers)-1):
            w = np.random.randn(self.layers[i+1], self.layers[i])
            b = np.random.randn(self.layers[i+1], 1)
            self.weights.append(w)
            self.biases.append(b)

    def activation(self, z):
        # Here we use the sigmoid activation function as an example.
        return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
    
    def forward(self, x):
        """
        Forward propagate an input through the network.
        x should be a column vector (numpy array of shape (input_size, 1))
        Returns the output of the network.
        """
        a = x
        for i, (w, b) in enumerate(zip(self.weights, self.biases)):
            z = np.dot(w, a) + b
            a = self.activation(z)
        return a

# ---------------------------

        self.neuron_radius = 20

        self.draw_network()
        
    def draw_network(self):
        layers = self.network_architecture
        n_layers = len(layers)

```python
    features_norm = normalize_and_center(features)
    predictions_norm = normalize_and_center(predictions) # Normalizes the single column

    # Compute dot product (equivalent to correlation for normalized vectors)
    # features_norm.T is (n_features, n_samples)
    # predictions_norm is (n_samples, 1)

    exposures = jnp.dot(features_norm.T, predictions_norm)
```

class FeaturePenalizer(BasePenalizer):
    """
    Feature penalization with TensorFlow.

    Source (by jrb): https://github.com/jonrtaylor/twitch/blob/master/FE_Clipping_Script.ipynb

    Source of first PyTorch implementation (by Michael Oliver / mdo): https://forum.numer.ai/t/model-diagnostics-feature-exposure/899/12

    :param max_exposure: Number in range [0...1] indicating how much to reduce max feature exposure to.
    :param pred_name: Prediction column name. Used for new column name. \n
    :param suffix: Optional suffix that is added to new column name.
    """
    def __init__(

        self,
        max_exposure: float,
        pred_name: str = "prediction",
        suffix: str = None,
    ):
        self.max_exposure = max_exposure
        self.pred_name = pred_name
        assert (
            0.0 <= max_exposure <= 1.0
        ), f"'max_exposure' should be a float in range [0...1]. Got '{self.max_exposure}'."
        new_col_name = (
            f"{self.pred_name}_penalized_{self.max_exposure}_{suffix}"
            if suffix
            else f"{self.pred_name}_penalized_{self.max_exposure}"
        )
        super().__init__(new_col_name=new_col_name)
        self.suffix = suffix

    def transform(self, X: pd.DataFrame, features: pd.DataFrame, era_series: pd.Series) -> np.array:
        """
        Main transform method.
        :param X: Input predictions to neutralize. 
        :param features: DataFrame with features for neutralization. 
        :param era_series: Series with era labels for each row in features. 
        Features, eras and the prediction column must all have the same length.
        :return: Penalized predictions.
        """

        assert len(X) == len(era_series), "Input predictions must have same length as eras."

            dataf=df, column=self.pred_name, neutralizers=list(features.columns)
        )

        neutralized = []

                scores, exposure_values, len(neutralizers), None

class FeaturePenalizer(BasePenalizer):
    """
    Feature penalization with TensorFlow.

    Source (by jrb): https://github.com/jonrtaylor/twitch/blob/master/FE_Clipping_Script.ipynb

    Source of first PyTorch implementation (by Michael Oliver / mdo): https://forum.numer.ai/t/model-diagnostics-feature-exposure/899/12

    :param max_exposure: Number in range [0...1] indicating how much to reduce max feature exposure to.
    :param pred_name: Prediction column name. Used for new column name. \n
    :param suffix: Optional suffix that is added to new column name.
    """
    def __init__(

        self,
        max_exposure: float,
        pred_name: str = "prediction",
        suffix: str = None,
    ):
        self.max_exposure = max_exposure
        self.pred_name = pred_name
        assert (
            0.0 <= max_exposure <= 1.0
        ), f"'max_exposure' should be a float in range [0...1]. Got '{self.max_exposure}'."
        new_col_name = (
            f"{self.pred_name}_penalized_{self.max_exposure}_{suffix}"
            if suffix
            else f"{self.pred_name}_penalized_{self.max_exposure}"
        )
        super().__init__(new_col_name=new_col_name)
        self.suffix = suffix

    def transform(self, X: pd.DataFrame, features: pd.DataFrame, era_series: pd.Series) -> np.array:
        """
        Main transform method.
        :param X: Input predictions to neutralize. 
        :param features: DataFrame with features for neutralization. 
        :param era_series: Series with era labels for each row in features. 
        Features, eras and the prediction column must all have the same length.
        :return: Penalized predictions.
        """
        assert len(X) == len(features), "Input predictions must have same length as features."
        assert len(X) == len(era_series), "Input predictions must have same length as eras."
        df = features.copy()
        df["prediction"] = X
        df["era"] = era_series
        penalized_data = self._reduce_all_exposures(
            dataf=df, column=self.pred_name, neutralizers=list(features.columns)
        )
        return penalized_data

    def _reduce_all_exposures(
        self,
        dataf: pd.DataFrame,
        column: str = "prediction",
        neutralizers: list = None,
        normalize=True,
        gaussianize=True,
    ) -> pd.DataFrame:
        neutralized = []

        for era in tqdm(dataf["era"].unique()):
            dataf_era = dataf[dataf["era"] == era]
            scores = dataf_era[[column]].values
            exposure_values = dataf_era[neutralizers].values

            if normalize:
                scores2 = []
                for x in scores.T:
                    x = (scipy.stats.rankdata(x, method="ordinal") - 0.5) / len(x)
                    if gaussianize:
                        x = scipy.stats.norm.ppf(x)
                    scores2.append(x)
                scores = np.array(scores2)[0]

            scores, _ = self._reduce_exposure(
                scores, exposure_values, len(neutralizers), None
            )

            scores /= tf.math.reduce_std(scores)
            scores -= tf.reduce_min(scores)
            scores /= tf.reduce_max(scores)
            neutralized.append(scores.numpy())

        predictions = pd.DataFrame(
            np.concatenate(neutralized), columns=[column], index=dataf.index
        )
        return predictions

    def _reduce_exposure(self, prediction, features, input_size=50, weights=None):
        model = tf.keras.models.Sequential(
            [
                tf.keras.layers.Input(input_size),
                tf.keras.experimental.LinearModel(use_bias=False),
            ]
        )
        feats = tf.convert_to_tensor(features - 0.5, dtype=tf.float32)
        pred = tf.convert_to_tensor(prediction, dtype=tf.float32)
        if weights is None:
            optimizer = tf.keras.optimizers.Adamax()
            start_exp = self.__exposures(feats, pred[:, None])
            target_exps = tf.clip_by_value(
                start_exp, -self.max_exposure, self.max_exposure
            )
            self._train_loop(model, optimizer, feats, pred, target_exps)
        else:
            model.set_weights(weights)
        return pred[:, None] - model(feats), model.get_weights()

    def _train_loop(self, model, optimizer, feats, pred, target_exps):
        for _ in range(1000000):
            loss, grads = self.__train_loop_body(model, feats, pred, target_exps)
            optimizer.apply_gradients(zip(grads, model.trainable_variables))
            if loss < 1e-7:
                break

    def __train_loop_body(self, model, feats, pred, target_exps):
        with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
            exps = self.__exposures(feats, pred[:, None] - model(feats, training=True))
            loss = tf.reduce_sum(
                tf.nn.relu(tf.nn.relu(exps) - tf.nn.relu(target_exps))
                + tf.nn.relu(tf.nn.relu(-exps) - tf.nn.relu(-target_exps))
            )
        return loss, tape.gradient(loss, model.trainable_variables)

    @staticmethod
    def __exposures(x, y):
        x = x - tf.math.reduce_mean(x, axis=0)
        x = x / tf.norm(x, axis=0)
        y = y - tf.math.reduce_mean(y, axis=0)
        y = y / tf.norm(y, axis=0)
        return tf.matmul(x, y, transpose_a=True)

To create a Kubernetes namespace using Ansible, you can use the `community.kubernetes.k8s` module. Below is a step-by-step guide:

---

### 1. **Install Required Ansible Collection**
Ensure the `community.kubernetes` collection is installed:

```bash
ansible-galaxy collection install community.kubernetes
```

You may also need the `openshift` Python client library:

```bash
pip install openshift
```

---

### 2. **Create an Ansible Playbook**
Create a playbook (e.g., `create-namespace.yml`):

```yaml
---
- name: Create Kubernetes Namespace
  hosts: localhost  # Run on the Ansible control node
  connection: local
  vars:
    namespace_name: "my-namespace"  # Replace with your namespace name
    kubeconfig: "~/.kube/config"    # Path to your kubeconfig file

  tasks:
    - name: Ensure namespace exists
      community.kubernetes.k8s:
        api_version: v1
        kind: Namespace
        name: "{{ namespace_name }}"
        state: present
        kubeconfig: "{{ kubeconfig }}"
```

---

### 3. **Run the Playbook**
Execute the playbook:

```bash
ansible-playbook create-namespace.yml
```

---

### 4. **Verify the Namespace**
Check if the namespace was created:

```bash
kubectl get namespaces
```

---

### Key Notes:
- **Authentication**: The playbook uses the `kubeconfig` file (default: `~/.kube/config`). Ensure your Ansible control node has access to the cluster.
- **Idempotency**: The task is idempotent—running it multiple times won’t create duplicate namespaces.
- **Advanced Auth**: If using token-based authentication, use the `api_key`, `host`, and `validate_certs` parameters in the `k8s` module.

---

### Example with In-Cluster Authentication (e.g., running in a Pod):

```python
import math
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def create_rounded_key_boundary(x_center, y_center, width, height, radius, points_per_corner=15):
    """
    Generates the (x, y) coordinates for the boundary of a rounded rectangle key,
    centered at (x_center, y_center). Uses mathematical functions for curves and lines.
    """
    # Calculate half dimensions for easier centering
    half_w = width / 2
    half_h = height / 2

    # Ensure radius is not too large
    radius = min(radius, half_w, half_h)

    # Calculate corner circle centers relative to the key center
    # Top-right, top-left, bottom-left, bottom-right
    centers_rel = [
        (half_w - radius, half_h - radius),  # TR
        (-half_w + radius, half_h - radius), # TL
        (-half_w + radius, -half_h + radius),# BL
        (half_w - radius, -half_h + radius)  # BR
    ]

    # Define angle ranges for the corners (radians)
    # TR: 0 to pi/2
    # TL: pi/2 to pi
    # BL: pi to 3pi/2
    # BR: 3pi/2 to 2pi (or -pi/2 to 0)
    angle_ranges = [
        np.linspace(0, math.pi / 2, points_per_corner),
        np.linspace(math.pi / 2, math.pi, points_per_corner),
        np.linspace(math.pi, 3 * math.pi / 2, points_per_corner),
        np.linspace(3 * math.pi / 2, 2 * math.pi, points_per_corner)
    ]

    all_x = []
    all_y = []

    # Generate points for corners and straight edges connecting them
    # Start from the middle of the right edge and go clockwise

    # Right edge (top part)
    all_x.append(x_center + half_w)
    all_y.append(y_center + half_h - radius)

    # Top-right corner (using sin/cos - trigonometric math functions)
    cx, cy = centers_rel[0]
    angles = angle_ranges[0]
    all_x.extend(x_center + cx + radius * np.cos(angles))
    all_y.extend(y_center + cy + radius * np.sin(angles))

    # Top edge (using linear function implicitly by connecting points)
    # Connects end of TR arc to start of TL arc
    # Start point: (x_center + half_w - radius, y_center + half_h)
    # End point:   (x_center - half_w + radius, y_center + half_h)
    # (Intermediate points could be added with np.linspace for true mathematical line)
    all_x.append(x_center - half_w + radius)
    all_y.append(y_center + half_h)


    # Top-left corner
    cx, cy = centers_rel[1]
    angles = angle_ranges[1]
    all_x.extend(x_center + cx + radius * np.cos(angles))
    all_y.extend(y_center + cy + radius * np.sin(angles))

    # Left edge
    all_x.append(x_center - half_w)
    all_y.append(y_center - half_h + radius)

    # Bottom-left corner
    cx, cy = centers_rel[2]
    angles = angle_ranges[2]
    all_x.extend(x_center + cx + radius * np.cos(angles))
    all_y.extend(y_center + cy + radius * np.sin(angles))

    # Bottom edge
    all_x.append(x_center + half_w - radius)
    all_y.append(y_center - half_h)

    # Bottom-right corner
    cx, cy = centers_rel[3]
    angles = angle_ranges[3]
    all_x.extend(x_center + cx + radius * np.cos(angles))
    all_y.extend(y_center + cy + radius * np.sin(angles))

    # Close the loop by connecting back to the start of the right edge
    all_x.append(x_center + half_w)
    all_y.append(y_center + half_h - radius)


    return all_x, all_y
```

# w,h are the width and height. r is the “corner radius”.
def rounded_key_boundary(x0, y0, w, h, r, pts_per_corner=20):
    # Make sure the corner radius is not too big:
    r = min(r, w/2, h/2)
    
    # Calculate centers of the four quarter‐circles
    # Bottom-left, bottom-right, top-right, top-left
    centers = [
        (x0 + r, y0 + r),             # bottom-left
        (x0 + w - r, y0 + r),         # bottom-right
        (x0 + w - r, y0 + h - r),     # top-right
        (x0 + r, y0 + h - r)          # top-left
    ]
    
    # For each corner the arc sweep:
    # bottom-left: angles from pi to 3pi/2
    # bottom-right: from 3pi/2 to 2pi
    # top-right: from 0 to pi/2
    # top-left: from pi/2 to pi
    arc_angles = [
        np.linspace(math.pi, 1.5*math.pi, pts_per_corner, endpoint=False),
        np.linspace(1.5*math.pi, 2*math.pi, pts_per_corner, endpoint=False),
        np.linspace(0, 0.5*math.pi, pts_per_corner, endpoint=False),
        np.linspace(0.5*math.pi, math.pi, pts_per_corner, endpoint=False)
    ]
    
    # Build the boundary points in order by having each arc then the connecting straight segment.
    boundary_x = []
    boundary_y = []
    
    # For each corner, compute the arc and then add a straight segment to the next corner.
    for i in range(4):
        cx, cy = centers[i]
        # compute arc points:
        angles = arc_angles[i]
        for angle in angles:
            boundary_x.append(cx + r * math.cos(angle))
            boundary_y.append(cy + r * math.sin(angle))
        
        # After finishing the arc, add a straight edge connecting to the next arc.
        # The next arc’s start is at an angle in the next corner (we consider modulo 4).
        next_i = (i+1) % 4
        # For the straight edge, we can use one intermediate point: the endpoint of current arc
        # and the start point of the next arc. (They are separated by a straight line.)
        # For instance, after bottom-left arc, the next arc is bottom-right so we draw the bottom edge.
        if i == 0:  
            # bottom edge: from (x0+r, y0) to (x0+w-r, y0)
            x_start = x0 + r
            x_end   = x0 + w - r
            # simply add the endpoint (the next arc will generate its corner)
            # (Only if there is a gap – add a few intermediate points so that the edge is drawn mathematically)
            steps = np.linspace(x_start, x_end, 10, endpoint=False)[1:]
            for xs in steps:
                boundary_x.append(xs)
                boundary_y.append(y0)
        elif i == 1:
            # right edge: from (x0+w, y0+r) to (x0+w, y0+h-r)
            y_start = y0 + r
            y_end   = y0 + h - r
            steps = np.linspace(y_start, y_end, 10, endpoint=False)[1:]
            for ys in steps:

                boundary_y.append(ys)
        elif i == 2:
            # top edge: from (x0+w-r, y0+h) to (x0+r, y0+h)
            x_start = x0 + w - r
            x_end   = x0 + r
            steps = np.linspace(x_start, x_end, 10, endpoint=False)[1:]
            for xs in steps:
                boundary_x.append(xs)
                boundary_y.append(y0+h)
        elif i == 3:
            # left edge: from (x0, y0+h-r) to (x0, y0+r)
            y_start = y0 + h - r
            y_end   = y0 + r
            steps = np.linspace(y_start, y_end, 10, endpoint=False)[1:]
            for ys in steps:
                boundary_x.append(x0)
                boundary_y.append(ys)
    
    # Close the boundary by returning to the first point:
    boundary_x.append(boundary_x[0])
    boundary_y.append(boundary_y[0])
    return boundary_x, boundary_y

# Now, let’s draw a keyboard layout.

def rounded_key_boundary(x0, y0, w, h, r, pts_per_corner=20):
    # Make sure the corner radius is not too big:

    # Bottom-left, bottom-right, top-right, top-left

        (x0 + w - r, y0 + r),         # bottom-right

// Function to find the index of the array element that is strictly less than target.

int findIndex(int arr[], int n, int target) {

    int ans = -1;  // This will hold the result index

{
    GENERATED_BODY()

public:
    AMyGameMode();

    virtual void BeginPlay() override;
    virtual void Tick(float DeltaSeconds) override;

    // A shared pointer to an audio capture device
    TSharedPtr<IAudioCapture> AudioCaptureDevice;

{
    // Enable ticking if you intend to poll/process audio data
    PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick = true;
}

void AMyGameMode::BeginPlay()
{
    Super::BeginPlay();

    // Create our AudioCapture device. FAudioCapture::Create() returns a TSharedPtr<IAudioCapture>.
    AudioCaptureDevice = FAudioCapture::Create();
    if (AudioCaptureDevice.IsValid())
    {
        // Set up our capture parameters.
        // (Using the default device by setting DeviceIndex to INDEX_NONE)
        IAudioCapture::FCaptureParams CaptureParams;
        CaptureParams.DeviceIndex = INDEX_NONE;  // use the default audio input device
        CaptureParams.SampleRate  = 44100;         // set the sample rate (adjust as needed)
        CaptureParams.NumChannels = 2;             // set the number of channels (e.g., 2 for stereo)
        CaptureParams.Callback    = nullptr;       // no callback provided – you could assign one here if desired

        // Open the audio capture stream with these parameters.
        if (AudioCaptureDevice->OpenStream(CaptureParams))
        {
            UE_LOG(LogTemp, Log, TEXT("Audio capture stream opened successfully."));

            // Start the capture stream.
            AudioCaptureDevice->StartStream();
        }
        else
        {
            UE_LOG(LogTemp, Error, TEXT("Failed to open audio capture stream."));
        }
    }
    else
    {
        UE_LOG(LogTemp, Error, TEXT("Failed to create audio capture device!"));
    }

Begin your evaluation by generating your own answer to the prompt. You must provide your answers before judging any answers.

When evaluating the assistants' answers, compare both assistants' answers with your answer. You must identify and correct any mistakes or inaccurate information.

Then consider if the assistant's answers are helpful, relevant, and concise. Helpful means the answer correctly responds to the prompt or follows the instructions. Note when user prompt has any ambiguity or more than one interpretation, it is more helpful and appropriate to ask for clarifications or more information from the user than providing an answer based on assumptions. Relevant means all parts of the response closely connect or are appropriate to what is being asked. Concise means the response is clear and not verbose or excessive.

Then consider the creativity and novelty of the assistant's answers when needed. Finally, identify any missing important information in the assistants' answers that would be beneficial to include when responding to the user prompt.

After providing your explanation, you must output only one of the following choices as your final verdict with a label:

1. Assistant A is significantly better: [[A>>B]]
2. Assistant A is slightly better: [[A>B]]
3. Tie, relatively the same: [[A=B]]
4. Assistant B is slightly better: [[B>A]]
5. Assistant B is significantly better: [[B>>A]]

Example output: "My final verdict is tie: [[A=B]]".

import { prisma } from "@/utils/prisma";
import { z } from "zod";
import { FastifyPluginAsyncTypeProvider } from "@/utils/fastify";
import {
  serializerCompiler,
  validatorCompiler,
} from "fastify-type-provider-zod";
import { validateRequestPassword } from "@/utils/password";
import { changePassword } from "@/utils/user";
import { validateAuthUser } from "@/utils/authCheck";
import bcrypt from "bcrypt";

const updateUserPasswordSchema = z.object({
  password: z.string(),
  new_password: z.string(),
  new_password_confirmation: z.string(),
});

const index: FastifyPluginAsyncTypeProvider = async (fastify) => {
  fastify.setSerializerCompiler(serializerCompiler);
  fastify.setValidatorCompiler(validatorCompiler);
  fastify.patch(
    "/",
    {
      schema: {
        body: updateUserPasswordSchema,
      },
    },
    async (request, reply) => {
      const authedUser = validateAuthUser(request.user);

      const userData = await prisma.users.findUnique({
        where: { id: authedUser.id },
      });
      if (!userData) {
        throw fastify.httpErrors.notFound("ユーザー情報がありません");
      }

      const result = await new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
        bcrypt.compare(request.body.password, userData.password, (err, res) => {
          if (err) {
            reject(fastify.httpErrors.internalServerError());
          } else {
            resolve(res);
          }
        });
      });

      if (!result) {
        throw fastify.httpErrors.badRequest("現在のパスワードが異なります");
      }

      if (request.body.password === request.body.new_password) {
        throw fastify.httpErrors.badRequest(
          "新しいパスワードは現在のパスワードと違うものを入力してください"
        );
      } else if (
        request.body.new_password !== request.body.new_password_confirmation
      ) {
        throw fastify.httpErrors.badRequest("新しいパスワードが一致しません");
      }

      await changePassword({
        user_id: authedUser.id,
        password: request.body.new_password,
      });

      reply.send("OK");
    }
  );
};

export default index;

"use strict";
import { prisma } from "@/utils/prisma";
import { z } from "zod";
import { FastifyPluginAsyncTypeProvider } from "@/utils/fastify";
import {
  serializerCompiler,
  validatorCompiler,
} from "fastify-type-provider-zod";
import { validateRequestPassword } from "@/utils/password";
import { changePassword } from "@/utils/user";
import { validateAuthUser } from "@/utils/authCheck";
import bcrypt from "bcrypt";

// 入力スキーマの定義
const updateUserPasswordSchema = z.object({
  password: z.string(),
  new_password: z.string(),
  new_password_confirmation: z.string(),
});

// パスワードチェックのためのラッパー関数
async function verifyPassword(
  plainPassword: string,
  hashedPassword: string,
  httpErrors: any
): Promise<boolean> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    bcrypt.compare(plainPassword, hashedPassword, (err, result) => {
      if (err) {
        return reject(httpErrors.internalServerError());
      }
      resolve(result);
    });
  });
}

const updateUserPasswordRoute: FastifyPluginAsyncTypeProvider = async (fastify) => {
  fastify.setSerializerCompiler(serializerCompiler);
  fastify.setValidatorCompiler(validatorCompiler);

  // PATCH / エンドポイント：ユーザーのパスワード変更
  fastify.patch(
    "/",
    {
      schema: {
        body: updateUserPasswordSchema,
      },
    },
    async (request, reply) => {
      // 認証済みユーザーの取得と検証
      const authUser = validateAuthUser(request.user);

      // ユーザー情報が存在するか確認
      const userData = await prisma.users.findUnique({
        where: { id: authUser.id },
      });
      if (!userData) {
        throw fastify.httpErrors.notFound("ユーザー情報がありません");
      }

      // 入力された現在のパスワードとDBに保存されているパスワードの比較
      const isPasswordCorrect = await verifyPassword(
        request.body.password,
        userData.password,
        fastify.httpErrors
      );

      if (!isPasswordCorrect) {
        throw fastify.httpErrors.badRequest("現在のパスワードが異なります");
      }

      // 新しいパスワードが現在のパスワードと同じ場合、または新パスワードと確認用パスワードが一致しない場合のエラー処理
      if (request.body.password === request.body.new_password) {
        throw fastify.httpErrors.badRequest(
          "新しいパスワードは現在のパスワードと違うものを入力してください"
        );
      }
      if (request.body.new_password !== request.body.new_password_confirmation) {
        throw fastify.httpErrors.badRequest("新しいパスワードが一致しません");
      }

      // パスワード更新処理
      await changePassword({
        user_id: authUser.id,
        password: request.body.new_password,
      });

      reply.send("OK");
    }
  );
};

export default updateUserPasswordRoute;

1. 変数名を意味のある名前に変更

```typescript
import { prisma } from "@/utils/prisma";
import { z } from "zod";
import { FastifyPluginAsyncTypeProvider } from "@/utils/fastify";
import {
  serializerCompiler,
  validatorCompiler,
} from "fastify-type-provider-zod";
import { changePassword } from "@/utils/user";
import { validateAuthUser } from "@/utils/authCheck";
import bcrypt from "bcrypt";

// 定数定義
const ERROR_MESSAGES = {
  USER_NOT_FOUND: "ユーザー情報がありません",
  CURRENT_PASSWORD_MISMATCH: "現在のパスワードが異なります",
  SAME_PASSWORD: "新しいパスワードは現在のパスワードと違うものを入力してください",
  PASSWORD_MISMATCH: "新しいパスワードが一致しません",
};

// Zodスキーマ
const PasswordUpdateSchema = z.object({
  password: z.string(),
  new_password: z.string(),
  new_password_confirmation: z.string(),
});

// パスワード検証関数
const validatePasswordRequirements = (
  currentPassword: string,
  newPassword: string,
  confirmation: string
) => {
  if (currentPassword === newPassword) {
    throw new Error(ERROR_MESSAGES.SAME_PASSWORD);
  }

  if (newPassword !== confirmation) {
    throw new Error(ERROR_MESSAGES.PASSWORD_MISMATCH);
  }
};

// ユーザー取得ヘルパー
const getUser = async (userId: string) => {
  const user = await prisma.users.findUnique({ where: { id: userId } });
  if (!user) throw new Error(ERROR_MESSAGES.USER_NOT_FOUND);
  return user;
};

const index: FastifyPluginAsyncTypeProvider = async (fastify) => {
  fastify.setSerializerCompiler(serializerCompiler);
  fastify.setValidatorCompiler(validatorCompiler);

  fastify.patch(
    "/",
    { schema: { body: PasswordUpdateSchema } },
    async (request, reply) => {
      try {
        const authUser = validateAuthUser(request.user);
        const {
          password: currentPassword,
          new_password: newPassword,
          new_password_confirmation: confirmation,
        } = request.body;

        // 新しいパスワードの要件検証
        validatePasswordRequirements(currentPassword, newPassword, confirmation);

        // ユーザー情報取得
        const user = await getUser(authUser.id);

        // 現在のパスワード検証
        const isPasswordValid = await bcrypt.compare(
          currentPassword,
          user.password
        );
        if (!isPasswordValid) {
          throw fastify.httpErrors.badRequest(
            ERROR_MESSAGES.CURRENT_PASSWORD_MISMATCH
          );
        }

        // パスワード更新
        await changePassword({
          user_id: authUser.id,
          password: newPassword,
        });

        return reply.send("OK");
      } catch (error) {
        if (error instanceof Error) {
          throw fastify.httpErrors.badRequest(error.message);
        }
        throw fastify.httpErrors.internalServerError();
      }
    }
  );
};

export default index;
```

主な改善点：

1. **定数の抽出**: エラーメッセージを定数化することで、一貫性と保守性を向上
2. **関数の分割**: パスワード検証とユーザー取得処理を別関数に分割
3. **エラーハンドリングの統一**: try-catchブロックで一括エラーハンドリング
4. **変数名の改善**: 意味の明確な変数名を使用（例: `userData` → `user`）
5. **検証順序の最適化**: コストの高いパスワード比較前に軽量なバリデーションを実行
6. **型安全性の向上**: エラータイプのチェックを追加
7. **非同期処理の改善**: bcrypt.compareをasync/awaitで直接処理
8. **コードの論理ブロック化**: 関連する処理を視覚的にグループ化

これらの変更により、処理の流れが明確になり、保守性と可読性が大幅に向上しています。

double linearInterpolate(double x, const vector<double>& x_original, const vector<double>& y_original) {
    int n = x_original.size();

    if (x <= x_original.front()) {

            return y_original[i] + t * (y_original[i+1] - y_original[i]);

    return 0.0;

```python
import os
```

```python
Pygame Hex Grid Demo

Demonstrates a basic hexagonal grid using Pygame,
with correct coordinate conversions (axial coordinates, pointy-top hexes)
and perfect tiling. Allows clicking to highlight a hex.
"""

import pygame
import math
import sys

# --- Constants ---
WIDTH, HEIGHT = 800, 600
HEX_SIZE = 30  # Radius from center to vertex
FPS = 60
SQRT3 = math.sqrt(3)

# Colors
COLOR_BG = (30, 30, 30)
COLOR_HEX_LINE = (100, 100, 100)
COLOR_HIGHLIGHT = (255, 50, 50)
COLOR_TEXT = (200, 200, 200)

# Grid Origin (center of the screen)
ORIGIN_X = WIDTH // 2
ORIGIN_Y = HEIGHT // 2

# Grid extent for drawing (adjust if needed for full screen coverage)
GRID_DRAW_RADIUS_Q = 15
GRID_DRAW_RADIUS_R = 15

# --- Hex Grid Functions (Axial Coordinates, Pointy-Top) ---

def hex_to_pixel(q, r, size=HEX_SIZE):
    """Converts axial hex coordinates (q, r) to pixel coordinates (x, y) relative to the grid origin."""
    x = size * SQRT3 * (q + r / 2.0)
    y = size * 1.5 * r
    return (x + ORIGIN_X, y + ORIGIN_Y)

def pixel_to_hex(x, y, size=HEX_SIZE):
    """Converts pixel coordinates (x, y) to axial hex coordinates (q, r)."""
    # Adjust for screen origin
    px = x - ORIGIN_X
    py = y - ORIGIN_Y

    # Calculate fractional axial coordinates
    q_frac = (SQRT3 / 3.0 * px - 1.0 / 3.0 * py) / size
    r_frac = (2.0 / 3.0 * py) / size

    return axial_round(q_frac, r_frac)

def axial_round(q_frac, r_frac):
    """Rounds fractional axial coordinates to the nearest integer hex coordinate tuple (q, r)."""
    # Convert to fractional cube coordinates (x, y, z) where x+y+z=0
    x_frac = q_frac
    z_frac = r_frac
    y_frac = -x_frac - z_frac

    # Round cube coordinates to nearest integers
    rx = round(x_frac)
    ry = round(y_frac)
    rz = round(z_frac)

    # Calculate differences
    x_diff = abs(rx - x_frac)
    y_diff = abs(ry - y_frac)
    z_diff = abs(rz - z_frac)

    # Reset the coordinate with the largest difference to maintain the constraint x+y+z=0
    if x_diff > y_diff and x_diff > z_diff:
        rx = -ry - rz
    elif y_diff > z_diff:
        ry = -rx - rz
    else:
        rz = -rx - ry

    # Convert rounded cube coordinates back to axial (q = x, r = z)
    return (rx, rz)

    """Calculates the 6 pixel coordinates for the vertices of a hex at (q, r)."""
    center_x, center_y = hex_to_pixel(q, r, size)
    corners = []
    for i in range(6):
        # Angle starts at -30 degrees (pointing east for the first corner) for pointy-top hexes
        angle_deg = 60 * i - 30
        angle_rad = math.radians(angle_deg)
        px = center_x + size * math.cos(angle_rad)
        py = center_y + size * math.sin(angle_rad)
        corners.append((px, py))
    return corners

# --- Pygame Setup ---
pygame.init()
screen = pygame.display.set_mode((WIDTH, HEIGHT))
pygame.display.set_caption("Hex Grid Wargame Base")
clock = pygame.time.Clock()
font = pygame.font.Font(None, 24) # Font for displaying coordinates

    mouse_pos = pygame.mouse.get_pos()

        for r in range(-GRID_DRAW_RADIUS_R, GRID_DRAW_RADIUS_R + 1):

            corners = get_hex_corners(q, r)
            
            # Draw hex outline
            pygame.draw.polygon(screen, COLOR_HEX_LINE, corners, 1)

            # Highlight selected hex
            if selected_hex is not None and (q, r) == selected_hex:
                pygame.draw.polygon(screen, COLOR_HIGHLIGHT, corners, 0) # Draw filled highlight

    # Display coordinates of selected hex

        coord_text = f"Selected: {selected_hex}"
        text_surf = font.render(coord_text, True, COLOR_TEXT)
        screen.blit(text_surf, (10, 10))
    # Display coordinates of hex under mouse
```

"""
Hex-Based Wargame in PyGame
---------------------------
This script uses a hex grid (pointy-topped hexes) that tiles the plane perfectly.
The key functions are:
  • hex_to_pixel(q, r, size, origin): converts an axial coordinate (q, r)
    into a pixel coordinate.

import pygame
import math
import sys

# ───── Configuration ───────────────────────────────

FPS = 30

# Pre-calc constant: square root of 3.

# The origin of the hex grid on screen (center the grid)

    Convert axial hex coordinates (q, r) to pixel coordinates.
    For pointy-topped orientation the formulas are:

      y = size * 3/2 * r
    Then we add the origin offset.
    """
    x = size * SQRT3 * (q + r / 2)
    y = size * 1.5 * r
    return (x + origin[0], y + origin[1])

    First shift by origin, then reverse the hex_to_pixel computation:
      q = (sqrt(3)/3 * x' - 1/3 * y') / size
      r = (2/3 * y') / size

    x -= origin[0]
    y -= origin[1]

    q = (SQRT3 / 3 * x - 1.0 / 3 * y) / size
    r = (2.0 / 3 * y) / size

    cube_z = r

    Making sure that x + y + z == 0 is maintained.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Hex-Based Wargame in PyGame
---------------------------
This script uses a hex grid (pointy-topped hexes) that tiles the plane perfectly.
The key functions are:
  • hex_to_pixel(q, r, size, origin): converts an axial coordinate (q, r)
    into a pixel coordinate.
  • pixel_to_hex(x, y, size, origin): does the inverse conversion (with
    proper rounding to the nearest hex coordinate).
  
Clicking the mouse will highlight the hex under the pointer.
"""

import pygame
import math
import sys

# ───── Configuration ───────────────────────────────
WIDTH, HEIGHT = 800, 600
FPS = 30

# The size (radius) of each hex.
HEX_SIZE = 30

# Pre-calc constant: square root of 3.
SQRT3 = math.sqrt(3)

# Define the grid extents in axial coordinates.
# We cover a wide range so that all hexes filling the screen are drawn.
GRID_RADIUS = 10

# The origin of the hex grid on screen (center the grid)
ORIGIN = (WIDTH // 2, HEIGHT // 2)


# ───── Hex Geometry & Coordinate Conversion Functions ─────────────
def hex_to_pixel(q, r, size=HEX_SIZE, origin=ORIGIN):
    """
    Convert axial hex coordinates (q, r) to pixel coordinates.
    For pointy-topped orientation the formulas are:
      x = size * sqrt3 * (q + r/2)
      y = size * 3/2 * r
    Then we add the origin offset.
    """
    x = size * SQRT3 * (q + r / 2)
    y = size * 1.5 * r
    return (x + origin[0], y + origin[1])


def pixel_to_hex(x, y, size=HEX_SIZE, origin=ORIGIN):
    """
    Convert pixel coordinates (x, y) to axial hex coordinates (q, r).
    First shift by origin, then reverse the hex_to_pixel computation:
      q = (sqrt(3)/3 * x' - 1/3 * y') / size
      r = (2/3 * y') / size
    Because the result is fractional, we round to the nearest axial coordinate.
    """
    # shift by origin
    x -= origin[0]
    y -= origin[1]
    
    # Fractional axial coordinates.
    q = (SQRT3 / 3 * x - 1.0 / 3 * y) / size
    r = (2.0 / 3 * y) / size

    # Convert axial to cube coordinates for proper rounding.
    cube_x = q
    cube_z = r
    cube_y = -cube_x - cube_z

    rx, ry, rz = cube_round(cube_x, cube_y, cube_z)
    # Convert cube back to axial (q, r) where q = cube_x, r = cube_z.
    return (rx, rz)


def cube_round(x, y, z):
    """
    Rounds floating point cube coordinates (x,y,z) to the nearest integer cube coordinate.
    Making sure that x + y + z == 0 is maintained.
    """
    rx = round(x)
    ry = round(y)
    rz = round(z)

    x_diff = abs(rx - x)
    y_diff = abs(ry - y)
    z_diff = abs(rz - z)

    if x_diff > y_diff and x_diff > z_diff:
        rx = -ry - rz
    elif y_diff > z_diff:
        ry = -rx - rz
    else:
        rz = -rx - ry
    return rx, ry, rz


def hex_corners(q, r, size=HEX_SIZE, origin=ORIGIN):
    """
    Return the six pixel coordinates of the corners of the hex at axial coordinate (q,r).
    The corners are computed around the center given by hex_to_pixel(q, r).
    Angle 0 is to the right; we calculate every 60 degrees.
    """
    cx, cy = hex_to_pixel(q, r, size, origin)
    corners = []
    for i in range(6):
        angle_rad = math.radians(60 * i - 30)  # offset to align pointy top
        x = cx + size * math.cos(angle_rad)
        y = cy + size * math.sin(angle_rad)
        corners.append((x, y))
    return corners


# ───── PyGame Setup and Main Loop ─────────────────────────────
def main():
    pygame.init()
    screen = pygame.display.set_mode((WIDTH, HEIGHT))
    pygame.display.set_caption("Hex-Based Wargame")
    clock = pygame.time.Clock()

    # For demonstration, store a highlighted hex coordinate that gets selected by clicking.
    highlighted_hex = None

    running = True
    while running:
        for event in pygame.event.get():
            if event.type == pygame.QUIT:

                mx, my = pygame.mouse.get_pos()
                highlighted_hex = pixel_to_hex(mx, my)
                print(f"Clicked pixel: ({mx}, {my}) -> Hex: {highlighted_hex}")

        # Draw grid. We iterate over a range of axial coordinates.

        for q in range(-GRID_RADIUS, GRID_RADIUS + 1):
            for r in range(-GRID_RADIUS, GRID_RADIUS + 1):
                # Optionally, one could skip hexes that are far away.
                corners = hex_corners(q, r)
                # Draw the hex outline in gray.
                pygame.draw.polygon(screen, (100, 100, 100), corners, 1)
                # Optionally fill a hex if it is the highlighted one.
                if highlighted_hex is not None and (q, r) == highlighted_hex:
                    pygame.draw.polygon(screen, (200, 50, 50), corners, 0)

        pygame.display.flip()
        clock.tick(FPS)

    pygame.quit()
    sys.exit()


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

*   **Unit Safety Officer:** Verify compliance with safety standards (MIL-STD-882E, TB 43-0134) and conduct risk assessments for the cleaning area/process.

**5.0 MATERIALS AND EQUIPMENT:**
*   **Personal Protective Equipment (PPE):**
    *   Eye Protection: ANSI Z87.1 compliant safety glasses or goggles (face shield recommended if using pressure washer).
    *   Hand Protection: Chemical-resistant gloves (e.g., Nitrile, Neoprene) appropriate for cleaning agents used.

    *   Footwear: Approved safety boots.

    *   Secondary (Optional, for heavy grease/oil): Approved degreaser (e.g., MIL-PRF-680 Type II, used sparingly and only on affected areas, followed by thorough rinsing). *Caution: Solvents can degrade rubber; use requires specific approval and justification.*
*   **Tools & Equipment:**
    *   Water Source: Hose with adjustable nozzle or pressure washer (pressure NOT to exceed 1200 PSI at the nozzle and maintain minimum distance of 12 inches from tire surface – consult TM for specific limits).
    *   Brushes: Assortment of non-metallic, stiff and medium-bristle brushes (long handle recommended). Avoid wire brushes.
    *   Buckets: For mixing cleaning solutions.
    *   Scraper/Pry Tool: Non-metallic/non-sparking, for removing caked mud/debris.
    *   Compressed Air Source (Optional): Low pressure (≤ 30 PSI) for drying crevices.
    *   Containment: Portable wash rack or designated wash bay with oil/water separator and appropriate drainage/containment system compliant with environmental regulations.
    *   Waste Receptacles: Clearly labeled containers for HAZWASTE (contaminated rags, effluent if not drained to separator).
    *   Lighting: Adequate task lighting if required.
    *   Chocks: Wheel chocks compliant with vehicle weight.
*   **Documentation:** DA Form 5988-E/2404, Logbook, Pen.

**6.0 PROCEDURE:**

**6.1 Preparation & Safety:**
    6.1.1 Conduct Pre-Task Safety Briefing: Review hazards (slips, chemical exposure, high-pressure water), required PPE, SDS information, and emergency procedures.
    6.1.2 Position Rover: Move rover to designated, level cleaning area (wash rack/bay).
    6.1.3 Secure Rover: Engage parking brake, place transmission in Park/Neutral, shut down engine, and place wheel chocks securely fore and aft of at least one non-driven, non-steered wheel (or per vehicle TM).
    6.1.4 Prepare Cleaning Area: Ensure adequate drainage/containment, clear obstructions, and stage all required materials and equipment. Review SDS for selected cleaning agents.
    6.1.5 Don Required PPE: Verify PPE is serviceable and worn correctly.

**6.2 Pre-Cleaning Inspection & Gross Debris Removal:**
    6.2.1 Initial Tire Inspection: Visually inspect each tire (tread, sidewalls, bead area) for obvious damage (cuts, punctures, blisters, embedded objects, excessive/uneven wear). Note findings on DA Form 5988-E/2404. Tag tires requiring immediate repair per TM.
    6.2.2 Remove Gross Debris: Using gloved hands or a non-metallic scraper, carefully remove large clumps of mud, rocks, vegetation, or other caked-on debris from treads and sidewalls. *Caution: Check for embedded sharp objects (nails, shrapnel) before handling.*

    6.3.1 Initial Rinse: Using low-pressure water (hose or pressure washer < 1200 PSI, >12” distance), thoroughly rinse each tire to remove loose dirt and saturate remaining contaminants. Work from top to bottom. Avoid prolonged, direct high-pressure spray on bead seals or valve stems.
    6.3.2 Apply Cleaning Agent: Mix approved detergent according to manufacturer's instructions and SDS in a bucket. Apply liberally to the entire tire surface (tread and both sidewalls) using a brush or low-pressure sprayer.

    6.3.5 Final Rinse: Rinse the tire thoroughly with ample low-pressure water, ensuring all detergent residue and loosened contaminants are removed. Check that runoff water is clear. Rinse surrounding wheel components as needed.

    6.4.1 Air Dry: Allow tires to air dry completely in a shaded area if possible (UV exposure can degrade rubber).
    6.4.2 Accelerated Drying (Optional): Use clean, lint-free rags to wipe excess water, or use low-pressure (≤ 30 PSI) compressed air, taking care not to force water into bead seals or bearings.

    6.5.1 Final Inspection: Once dry, re-inspect each tire thoroughly for cleanliness and any damage that may have been obscured by dirt (cuts, cracks, bulges, foreign objects). Verify bead seating area is clean. Check tire pressure and adjust per vehicle TM if necessary.

```kotlin
import java.util.* // Needed for sorting if not using built-in list sort functions explicitly

/*
Problem Breakdown:
- Input: a string `word` of lowercase English letters.
- Task: Remap letters 'a' through 'z' to telephone keys 2-9 to minimize total pushes needed to type `word`.
- Key Mapping Rules:
    - Keys 2-9 are available (8 keys total).
    - Each letter must map to exactly one key.
    - Multiple letters can map to the same key.
    - Cost to type a letter: 1 push if it's the 1st letter on its key, 2 pushes if it's the 2nd, etc.
- Goal: Find the minimum total pushes after optimal remapping.

Insight:
To minimize pushes, letters appearing most frequently in `word` should be assigned the lowest possible push cost.
Available "slots" and their costs:
- 8 slots with cost 1 (1st position on each of the 8 keys)
- 8 slots with cost 2 (2nd position on each of the 8 keys)
- 8 slots with cost 3 (3rd position on each of the 8 keys)
- ...

Algorithm:
1. Count the frequency of each character ('a' to 'z') in the input `word`.
2. Create a list containing the frequencies of characters that appear at least once in the word.
3. Sort this list of frequencies in descending order.
4. Iterate through the sorted frequencies. Assign a cost to each frequency based on its rank (position in the sorted list):
   - The first 8 frequencies (indices 0-7) correspond to letters that should get a cost of 1.
   - The next 8 frequencies (indices 8-15) correspond to letters that should get a cost of 2.
   - The next 8 frequencies (indices 16-23) correspond to letters that should get a cost of 3.
   - The remaining frequencies (indices 24-25, if they exist) correspond to letters that should get a cost of 4.
   - In general, the cost for the frequency at index `i` (0-based) in the sorted list is `floor(i / 8) + 1`.
5. Calculate the total minimum pushes by summing up `frequency * cost` for each element in the sorted frequency list.
6. Return the total sum.
*/

fun minimumPushes(word: String): Int {
    // 1. Count frequencies
    val counts = IntArray(26) { 0 } // Array to store counts for 'a' through 'z'
    for (char in word) {
        counts[char - 'a']++
    }

    // 2. Get non-zero frequencies and sort descendingly
    // Filter out characters that don't appear (count == 0)
    // Convert to list and sort in descending order
    val sortedFrequencies = counts.filter { it > 0 }.sortedDescending()

    // 3. Calculate total pushes based on sorted frequencies and assigned costs
    var totalPushes = 0
    for ((index, frequency) in sortedFrequencies.withIndex()) {
        // Calculate cost based on rank (index)
        // Index 0-7 -> cost 1
        // Index 8-15 -> cost 2
        // Index 16-23 -> cost 3
        // Index 24-25 -> cost 4
        val cost = (index / 8) + 1
        totalPushes += frequency * cost
    }

    // 4. Return the minimum total pushes
    return totalPushes
}
```

Here’s an outline of how you might do it:

──────────────────────────────
1. Create a RequestMatcher based on the Referer header

Spring Security provides RequestHeaderRequestMatcher which lets you match requests that have a particular header value. For example:

   RequestHeaderRequestMatcher matcher =
       new RequestHeaderRequestMatcher("Referer", "https://example.com/special");

This matcher will only match requests where the “Referer” header is exactly "https://example.com/special". (If you need a partial match or more complex logic, you can also write a custom RequestMatcher.)

──────────────────────────────
2. Define separate SecurityFilterChain beans

With multiple filter chains you tell Spring Security, “for requests that match this RequestMatcher, apply this filter chain”. For example:

   @Bean

       RequestHeaderRequestMatcher matcher =
           new RequestHeaderRequestMatcher("Referer", "https://example.com/special");

       http.requestMatcher(matcher)
           // For example, require authentication for all requests
           .authorizeRequests(authorize -> authorize.anyRequest().authenticated())
           // Add a custom filter before the UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter (or any filter of your choosing)
           .addFilterBefore(new CustomSpecialFilter(), UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)
           // ... further HttpSecurity settings

       return http.build();
   }

       http.authorizeRequests(authorize -> authorize.anyRequest().authenticated())

– The first chain (specialSecurityFilterChain) is only active when the Referer header exactly equals the specified URL.
– All other requests fall through to the default chain.

Spring Security will try each filter chain in order (based on @Order if specified or bean declaration order) and use the first one whose RequestMatcher matches.

──────────────────────────────
3. Considerations

• You can customize your RequestMatcher logic as needed. If the matching isn’t as straightforward as a simple equals you can write a custom RequestMatcher that does contains/regex checks on the Referer header.
• Remember that the Referer header is loosely controlled by the client—it’s possible for an attacker to supply a fake value. Use caution when basing security decisions solely on header content.
• Filter order matters. If you need to adjust the order of your chains, you can annotate your SecurityFilterChain beans with @Order or configure the bean order explicitly.

──────────────────────────────

If managing multiple filter chains isn’t convenient in your scenario, you could always create a custom filter that checks the Referer header and then conditionally applies some logic or delegates to different handlers. One common solution is to split your security configuration into multiple filter chains, each activated only when the incoming request has a specific Referer header value. In Spring Security you can do this by:

• Defining multiple SecurityFilterChain beans (available starting with Spring Security 5.x and Boot 2.1+),

Here’s an outline of how you might do it:

──────────────────────────────
1. Create a RequestMatcher based on the Referer header

Spring Security provides RequestHeaderRequestMatcher which lets you match requests that have a particular header value. For example:

   RequestHeaderRequestMatcher matcher =
       new RequestHeaderRequestMatcher("Referer", "https://example.com/special");

This matcher will only match requests where the “Referer” header is exactly "https://example.com/special". (If you need a partial match or more complex logic, you can also write a custom RequestMatcher.)

──────────────────────────────
2. Define separate SecurityFilterChain beans

With multiple filter chains you tell Spring Security, “for requests that match this RequestMatcher, apply this filter chain”. For example:

   @Bean
   public SecurityFilterChain specialSecurityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
       RequestHeaderRequestMatcher matcher =
           new RequestHeaderRequestMatcher("Referer", "https://example.com/special");

       http.requestMatcher(matcher)
           // For example, require authentication for all requests
           .authorizeRequests(authorize -> authorize.anyRequest().authenticated())
           // Add a custom filter before the UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter (or any filter of your choosing)
           .addFilterBefore(new CustomSpecialFilter(), UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)
           // ... further HttpSecurity settings
           ;

       return http.build();
   }

   @Bean
   public SecurityFilterChain defaultSecurityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
       // This chain can catch all other requests that don’t match your special chain.
       http.authorizeRequests(authorize -> authorize.anyRequest().authenticated())
           // Add a different custom filter if desired (or not)
           .addFilterBefore(new CustomDefaultFilter(), UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class);
       return http.build();
   }

In this example:
– The first chain (specialSecurityFilterChain) is only active when the Referer header exactly equals the specified URL.
– All other requests fall through to the default chain.

Spring Security will try each filter chain in order (based on @Order if specified or bean declaration order) and use the first one whose RequestMatcher matches.

──────────────────────────────
3. Considerations

• You can customize your RequestMatcher logic as needed. If the matching isn’t as straightforward as a simple equals you can write a custom RequestMatcher that does contains/regex checks on the Referer header.

Here are four approaches to improve Blender compositor line art edge detection, addressing the specific issues raised:

**Approach 1: Normal Pass - Neighbor Dot Product Variance**

*   **Description:** Instead of the potentially ambiguous dot product method described, this calculates the difference between a pixel's normal and its immediate neighbors. High variance indicates a sharp geometric change. This is better at capturing subtle normal map details than methods relying solely on the normal's orientation relative to a fixed vector.

On the other hand shadows get only edge outlined together with the meshes ofc and sharp color differences. I would like to have it separated or at least 1 perfect approach for the combined pass with only outlines for colors/light and shadows or the separated custom filter that won’t outline but make filled different color areas look like brushstrokes etc. Overall I need different combined/diffuse/albedo pass solution. Below is one strict‐format answer that details four updated/hybrid approaches. Each approach is explained with its math formulation and pseudocode, followed by at least two pros and two cons.

─────────────────────────────  
Approach 1: Enhanced Normal Pass with Adaptive Clamping  
─────────────────────────────  
Description:  
Instead of a simple dot‐product that “blows away” noisy but important details, use an adaptive clamping (or “soft threshold”) on the normal pass. The idea is to “squeeze” the values through a function that preserves subtler normal deviations while still keeping noisy parts in check.

Math Formulation:  
For each pixel with normal vector n, compute a directional difference with a chosen basis vector b (or a combination of bases). Then use:  

  edge_val = saturate( (|dot(n, b)| − T)^S )  

where  
  – T is a threshold (0 ≤ T ≤ 1),  
  – S is an exponential sensitivity factor, and  
  – saturate(x) clamps x to [0,1].

Pseudocode:  
--------------------------------------------------------  
function ComputeNormalEdge(n, b, T, S):  
  value = abs(dot(n, b))  
  edge = clamp((value - T) * S, 0, 1)  
  return edge  
--------------------------------------------------------  

Pros:  
• More control over the “faint line” details: you can capture more subtle edges by adjusting T and S.  
• Avoids entirely discarding noisy but useful detail (e.g. the “ice cream mode”) by reweighting rather than hard thresholding.

Cons:  
• Parameter tuning can become complex – S and T must be carefully chosen to balance detail vs. noise.  
• May amplify noise in regions where the normal variation is naturally high if S isn’t conservative enough.

─────────────────────────────  
Approach 2: Laplacian-Style Combined Pass Edge Detector  
─────────────────────────────  
Description:  
Replace your simple horizontal shifts with a Laplacian operator over the combined pass. Instead of subtracting one pixel left/right only, incorporate the four-neighbor differences to approximate a Laplacian, which naturally highlights rapid intensity changes (edges).

Math Formulation:  
For image intensity I(x, y), the discrete Laplacian can be expressed as:  

  L(x, y) = I(x+1, y) + I(x−1, y) + I(x, y+1) + I(x, y−1) − 4·I(x, y)  

Then the edge magnitude is:  

  Edge = clamp( |L(x, y)| · K, 0, 1)  

where K is a contrast amplification factor.

Pseudocode:  
--------------------------------------------------------  
for each pixel (x, y):  
  I_center = I(x, y)  
  I_right  = I(x+1, y)  
  I_left   = I(x−1, y)  
  I_up     = I(x, y+1)  
  I_down   = I(x, y−1)  
  lap = (I_right + I_left + I_up + I_down) - 4 * I_center  
  edge = clamp( abs(lap) * K, 0, 1)  
  store edge at (x, y)  
--------------------------------------------------------  

Pros:  
• Captures detail in all four cardinal directions instead of only horizontal differences, yielding a more robust edge map.  
• Better recovers fine detail in high-frequency regions without “flooding” uniform areas.

Cons:  
• Requires additional shifts (and possibly larger kernel sizes for diagonals) to avoid ghosting.  
• May generate additional artifacts if the underlying image contains noise or soft gradients.

─────────────────────────────  
Approach 3: Multi-Scale Difference-of-Gaussian (DoG) Edge Detection  
─────────────────────────────  
Description:  
Incorporate scale by comparing a minimally blurred image to one with a stronger Gaussian blur. This multi-scale approach, known as Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG), targets both subtle and pronounced edges. It works on combined image passes (diffuse, albedo, light) and can be tuned for sensitivity to texture versus sharp shadows.

Math Formulation:  
Let G(σ, I) denote a Gaussian blur on image I with standard deviation σ. Then:  

  Edge = |G(σ₁, I) − G(σ₂, I)|, with σ₂ > σ₁  

Optionally, a power transform may be applied:  

  Edge_out = (Edge)^α, then clamped to [0,1].

Pseudocode:  
--------------------------------------------------------  
G1 = GaussianBlur(I, sigma1)  
G2 = GaussianBlur(I, sigma2) // sigma2 > sigma1  
for each pixel (x, y):  
  diff = abs(G1(x, y) - G2(x, y))  
  edge = clamp(diff^α, 0, 1)  
  store edge at (x, y)  
--------------------------------------------------------  

Pros:  
• Flexibility in capturing both broad and fine details by adjusting σ₁, σ₂, and α.  
• Helps reduce spurious noise by leveraging the smoothing effect in the larger-scale blur.

Cons:  
• More computationally intensive (more blur passes, added parameter tuning).  
• May require careful calibration to ensure edges are not “washed out” or overly thick, especially in textured areas.

─────────────────────────────  
Approach 4: Hybrid Edge Mix (Normal + Diffuse) with Conditional Weighting  
─────────────────────────────  
Description:  
Fuse edge information derived separately from the normal pass and the combined (diffuse/albedo/light) pass. With conditional weighting, you can favor one domain (geometry vs. color/light contrasts) in different regions. For instance, the algorithm can use the normal-based edge detection for distinct geometry boundaries while falling back on the color-based DoG for texture details.

Math Formulation:  
Let:  

  E_normal = edge from enhanced normal pass  
  E_color  = edge from combined pass (e.g., DoG or Laplacian)  

Then mix them using a weight mask W that can be based on local variance or a preset threshold:  

  E_final = W · E_normal + (1 − W) · E_color  

For instance, W may be defined as:  

  W = step( variance_norm - V_threshold )  

or a smooth transition using a logistic function.

Pseudocode:  
--------------------------------------------------------  
for each pixel (x, y):  
  e_norm = ComputeNormalEdge(n(x,y), b, T, S)  
  e_color = ComputeCombinedEdge(I, x, y) // e.g., via Laplacian or DoG  
  W = ComputeWeight(variance(x, y), V_threshold) // returns value in [0,1]  
  E_final = clamp( W * e_norm + (1 - W) * e_color, 0, 1 )  
  store E_final at (x, y)  
--------------------------------------------------------  

Pros:  
• Offers the most flexibility by treating geometry and color/light details separately.  
• Detail separation enables non-uniform “line art” effects – for example, using strong normals for crisp boundaries and softer edges for painted or textured areas.

Cons:  
• Requires calibration of an additional weighting function and possibly more complex node arrangements.  
• Increases compositing complexity and may slow down processing if multiple passes are computed simultaneously.

─────────────────────────────  
Summary  
─────────────────────────────  
• Approach 1 refines your current normal-pass “dot product” method by adding adaptive clamping so you can keep subtle details without manual masking.  
• Approach 2 replaces simple subtraction with a Laplacian to capture multi-directional gradients in the combined pass.  
• Approach 3 introduces a multi-scale Difference-of-Gaussians method to allow detail capture at varying scales.  
• Approach 4 offers a hybrid solution that conditionally mixes geometry-based and color/light-based edges to tailor the final line art for different materials and lighting situations.

Each approach comes with its trade-offs; the best solution might even combine parts of more than one method, depending on the artistic look desired in your 3D render outlines—all achievable within Blender’s compositor using carefully built node networks.

### Approach 1: **Enhanced Normal Edge Detection via Neighbor Comparison**  
**Math**:  
For each pixel, compute dot product between its normal and shifted normals (left/right/up/down), then sum deviations:  
```
Edge = Σ_{dir} (1 - dot(N, N_shifted_dir))  
```  
**Pseudocode**:  
```
1. Normal Pass → Separate XYZ  
2. Duplicate Normal Pass → Shift Left/Right/Up/Down by 1px  
3. For each shifted normal:  
   - Dot product with original normal (Vector Math)  
   - Subtract from 1 (Math Node)  
4. Add all results → Power(2) → Square Root (optional)  
```  
**Pros**:  
- Captures subtle normal variations (e.g., wrinkles, bumps).  
- Reduces reliance on absolute normal magnitude.  
**Cons**:  
- Requires 4 shift operations (node-heavy).  
- May amplify noise in flat regions.  

---

### Approach 2: **Combined Pass Gradient Thresholding with Luminance Masking**  
**Math**:  
Compute gradient magnitude `G` from combined pass, then apply luminance-weighted threshold:  
```
G = sqrt((I_left - I)^2 + (I_right - I)^2)  
Threshold = (G > k * Luminance(I))  
```  
**Pseudocode**:  
```
1. Combined Pass → RGB to Luminance (L = 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B)  
2. Compute gradient magnitude (original method).  
3. Multiply luminance by scalar `k` → Compare with gradient (Math Node >).  
4. Use result as mask to isolate edges in bright areas.  
```  
**Pros**:  
- Avoids outlining filled bright regions (e.g., claws).  
- Automatically adapts to scene brightness.  
**Cons**:  
- Requires tuning `k` per scene.  
- May miss edges in dark, high-contrast regions.  

---

### Approach 3: **Multi-Scale Hybrid Edge Detection**  
**Math**:  
Fuse edges from normal and combined passes at multiple blur levels:  
```
E_final = max(E_combined, E_normal_high_freq, E_normal_low_freq)  
```  
**Pseudocode**:  
```
1. Normal Pass → Blur (Radius=2) → Process via Approach 1 → E_normal_low_freq  
2. Normal Pass → Process via Approach 1 → E_normal_high_freq  
3. Combined Pass → Process via Approach 2 → E_combined  
4. Use Z-Combine or Math (Maximum) to merge all edge maps.  
```  
**Pros**:  
- Captures both geometric and texture edges.  
- Balances detail and noise with multi-scale blur.  
**Cons**:  
- Very node-intensive.  
- Risk of overcompositing (double edges).  

---

### Approach 4: **Morphological Post-Processing for Line Refinement**  
**Math**:  
Apply morphological thinning to combined pass edges:  
```
E_thin = E - (E ⊖ kernel) ⊕ kernel  
```  
**Pseudocode**:  
```
1. Combined Pass → Compute gradient magnitude.  
2. Erode → Subtract from original → "Thicken" lines.  
3. Dilate → Subtract from thickened result → Isolate single-pixel edges.  
```  
**Pros**:  
- Produces crisp, thin lines.  
- Removes filled regions (e.g., belly texture).  
**Cons**:  
- Destroys weak edges (e.g., soft shadows).  
- Requires precise kernel sizing.  

---

### Final Recommendations:  
1. **For normal pass**: Use **Approach 1** with a **Color Ramp** set to "Constant" interpolation to clamp noise.  
2. **For combined pass**: Use **Approach 2** with a **Color Mix** node to blend with normal-based edges.  
3. Always pair with **Approach 4** to avoid filled regions.

    ```pseudocode
    6. Add Differences: Sum = Diff_L + Diff_R + Diff_U + Diff_D // Math node (Add) x3
    7. Optional: Apply Power node (e.g., exponent 2) for contrast. // Math node (Power)
    8. Optional: Use Color Ramp or Map Range node to clamp/scale result.
    ```

*   **Pros:**

    ```
    Edge = abs(Laplacian(I)) * contrast_scale
    ```
    Where `I` is the input image (Combined, Diffuse Color, etc.).

*   **Pseudocode:**
    ```pseudocode
    1. Get Input Pass (I) (e.g., Combined, Diffuse Color)
    2. Shift I Left/Right/Up/Down by 1px -> I_L, I_R, I_U, I_D // Translate node x4
    3. Add shifted images: Sum_Neighbors = I_L + I_R + I_U + I_D // Math node (Add) x3
    4. Multiply original I by 4: Four_I = 4 * I // Math node (Multiply)
    5. Subtract: Laplacian_Approx = Sum_Neighbors - Four_I // Math node (Subtract)
    6. Take Absolute Value: Edge = abs(Laplacian_Approx) // Math node (Absolute)
    7. Optional: Multiply by a scalar for contrast. // Math node (Multiply)
    8. Optional: Clamp values (e.g., using Color Ramp).
    ```

*   **Pros:**

*   **Cons:**

    *   Can sometimes produce double edges around smooth ramps.

**Approach 3: Difference of Gaussians (DoG) (Combined/Albedo/Diffuse Pass)**

This method finds edges by comparing two differently blurred versions of the image. It's good for finding features at specific scales and is more robust to noise than the Laplacian.

*   **Math:**
    ```
    G(I, sigma) = GaussianBlur(Image I, standard_deviation sigma)
    DoG(I, sigma1, sigma2) = G(I, sigma1) - G(I, sigma2)
    Edge = abs(DoG(I, sigma1, sigma2)) * contrast_scale
    ```
    Typically, `sigma2` is slightly larger than `sigma1` (e.g., `sigma2 = 1.6 * sigma1`).

*   **Pseudocode:**
    ```pseudocode
    1. Get Input Pass (I)
    2. Apply Gaussian Blur with sigma1 -> Blurred1 // Blur node (set Size = sigma1)
    3. Apply Gaussian Blur with sigma2 (sigma2 > sigma1) -> Blurred2 // Blur node (set Size = sigma2)
    4. Subtract: DoG = Blurred1 - Blurred2 // Math node (Subtract)
    5. Take Absolute Value: Edge = abs(DoG) // Math node (Absolute)
    6. Optional: Multiply by a scalar for contrast. // Math node (Multiply)
    7. Optional: Clamp/threshold values (e.g., using Color Ramp).
    ```

*   **Pros:**
    *   Acts as a band-pass filter, effective at finding edges/features at specific scales determined by `sigma1` and `sigma2`.
    *   More robust to noise than direct gradient or Laplacian methods due to the inherent blurring.
*   **Cons:**
    *   Requires two blur operations, potentially slower.
    *   Edge thickness depends on the sigma values; may not be as thin as Laplacian. Needs parameter tuning (`sigma1`, `sigma2`).

    ```
    Edge_Color = ComputeEdge_Color(ColorPass)   // e.g., using Approach 2 or 3

    L = Luminance(ColorPass)
    // Example: Decrease weight for color edges in bright areas
    ```

    `smoothstep(min, max, x)` provides a smooth transition from 0 to 1 as x goes from min to max. Can be approximated with Color Ramp node.

*   **Pseudocode (using Luminance to reduce Color Edge in bright areas):**
    ```pseudocode
    1. Compute Normal Edge map -> E_N (using Approach 1)
    2. Compute Color Edge map -> E_C (using Approach 2 or 3 on Diffuse Color or Combined pass)
    3. Get Color Pass used for E_C -> I_C
    4. Convert I_C to Luminance -> L // RGB to BW node
    5. Create Weight Mask W_color_edge: Use Color Ramp on L. Set black point at brightness threshold_low, white point at threshold_high. Invert the ramp output (so bright areas -> 0, dark areas -> 1). // Color Ramp node + Invert node
    6. Modulate Color Edge: E_C_Modulated = W_color_edge * E_C // Math node (Multiply)
    7. Combine: E_Final = max(E_N, E_C_Modulated) // Math node (Maximum)
    ```

*   **Pros:**
    *   Combines geometric structure (normals) with texture/lighting detail (color/combined).
    *   Weighting allows context-dependent line generation (e.g., suppressing unwanted edges from color pass in uniformly bright areas).
*   **Cons:**
    *   Most complex node setup, requires combining multiple edge detection pipelines.
    *   Requires careful tuning of the individual edge detection methods AND the weighting/blending strategy.

### Approach 1: **Enhanced Normal Edge Detection via Neighbor Comparison**  
**Math**:  
For each pixel, compute dot product between its normal and shifted normals (left/right/up/down), then sum deviations:  
```
Edge = Σ_{dir} (1 - dot(N, N_shifted_dir))  
```  
**Pseudocode**:  
```
1. Normal Pass → Separate XYZ  
2. Duplicate Normal Pass → Shift Left/Right/Up/Down by 1px  
3. For each shifted normal:  
   - Dot product with original normal (Vector Math)  
   - Subtract from 1 (Math Node)  
4. Add all results → Power(2) → Square Root (optional)  
```  
**Pros**:  
- Captures subtle normal variations (e.g., wrinkles, bumps).  
- Reduces reliance on absolute normal magnitude.  
**Cons**:  
- Requires 4 shift operations (node-heavy).  
- May amplify noise in flat regions.  

---

### Approach 2: **Combined Pass Gradient Thresholding with Luminance Masking**  
**Math**:  
Compute gradient magnitude `G` from combined pass, then apply luminance-weighted threshold:  
```
G = sqrt((I_left - I)^2 + (I_right - I)^2)  
Threshold = (G > k * Luminance(I))  
```  
**Pseudocode**:  
```
1. Combined Pass → RGB to Luminance (L = 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B)  
2. Compute gradient magnitude (original method).  
3. Multiply luminance by scalar `k` → Compare with gradient (Math Node >).  
4. Use result as mask to isolate edges in bright areas.  
```  
**Pros**:  
- Avoids outlining filled bright regions (e.g., claws).  
- Automatically adapts to scene brightness.  
**Cons**:  
- Requires tuning `k` per scene.  
- May miss edges in dark, high-contrast regions.  

---

### Approach 3: **Multi-Scale Hybrid Edge Detection**  
**Math**:  
Fuse edges from normal and combined passes at multiple blur levels:  
```
E_final = max(E_combined, E_normal_high_freq, E_normal_low_freq)  
```  
**Pseudocode**:  
```
1. Normal Pass → Blur (Radius=2) → Process via Approach 1 → E_normal_low_freq  
2. Normal Pass → Process via Approach 1 → E_normal_high_freq  
3. Combined Pass → Process via Approach 2 → E_combined  
4. Use Z-Combine or Math (Maximum) to merge all edge maps.  
```  
**Pros**:  
- Captures both geometric and texture edges.  
- Balances detail and noise with multi-scale blur.  
**Cons**:  
- Very node-intensive.  
- Risk of overcompositing (double edges).  

---

### Approach 4: **Morphological Post-Processing for Line Refinement**  
**Math**:  
Apply morphological thinning to combined pass edges:  
```
E_thin = E - (E ⊖ kernel) ⊕ kernel  
```  
**Pseudocode**:  
```
1. Combined Pass → Compute gradient magnitude.  
2. Erode → Subtract from original → "Thicken" lines.  
3. Dilate → Subtract from thickened result → Isolate single-pixel edges.  
```  
**Pros**:  
- Produces crisp, thin lines.  
- Removes filled regions (e.g., belly texture).  
**Cons**:  
- Destroys weak edges (e.g., soft shadows).  
- Requires precise kernel sizing.  

---

### Final Recommendations:  
1. **For normal pass**: Use **Approach 1** with a **Color Ramp** set to "Constant" interpolation to clamp noise.  
2. **For combined pass**: Use **Approach 2** with a **Color Mix** node to blend with normal-based edges.

Below is one strict‐format answer that details four updated/hybrid approaches. Each approach is explained with its math formulation and pseudocode, followed by at least two pros and two cons.

─────────────────────────────  
Approach 1: Enhanced Normal Pass with Adaptive Clamping  
─────────────────────────────  
Description:  
Instead of a simple dot‐product that “blows away” noisy but important details, use an adaptive clamping (or “soft threshold”) on the normal pass. The idea is to “squeeze” the values through a function that preserves subtler normal deviations while still keeping noisy parts in check.

Math Formulation:  
For each pixel with normal vector n, compute a directional difference with a chosen basis vector b (or a combination of bases). Then use:  

  edge_val = saturate( (|dot(n, b)| − T)^S )  

where  
  – T is a threshold (0 ≤ T ≤ 1),  
  – S is an exponential sensitivity factor, and  
  – saturate(x) clamps x to [0,1].

Pseudocode:  
--------------------------------------------------------  
function ComputeNormalEdge(n, b, T, S):  
  value = abs(dot(n, b))  
  edge = clamp((value - T) * S, 0, 1)  
  return edge  
--------------------------------------------------------  

Pros:  
• More control over the “faint line” details: you can capture more subtle edges by adjusting T and S.  
• Avoids entirely discarding noisy but useful detail (e.g. the “ice cream mode”) by reweighting rather than hard thresholding.

Cons:  
• Parameter tuning can become complex – S and T must be carefully chosen to balance detail vs. noise.  
• May amplify noise in regions where the normal variation is naturally high if S isn’t conservative enough.

─────────────────────────────  
Approach 2: Laplacian-Style Combined Pass Edge Detector  
─────────────────────────────  
Description:  
Replace your simple horizontal shifts with a Laplacian operator over the combined pass. Instead of subtracting one pixel left/right only, incorporate the four-neighbor differences to approximate a Laplacian, which naturally highlights rapid intensity changes (edges).

Math Formulation:  
For image intensity I(x, y), the discrete Laplacian can be expressed as:  

  L(x, y) = I(x+1, y) + I(x−1, y) + I(x, y+1) + I(x, y−1) − 4·I(x, y)  

Then the edge magnitude is:  

  Edge = clamp( |L(x, y)| · K, 0, 1)  

where K is a contrast amplification factor.

Pseudocode:  
--------------------------------------------------------  
for each pixel (x, y):  
  I_center = I(x, y)  
  I_right  = I(x+1, y)  
  I_left   = I(x−1, y)  
  I_up     = I(x, y+1)  
  I_down   = I(x, y−1)  
  lap = (I_right + I_left + I_up + I_down) - 4 * I_center  
  edge = clamp( abs(lap) * K, 0, 1)  
  store edge at (x, y)  
--------------------------------------------------------  

Pros:  
• Captures detail in all four cardinal directions instead of only horizontal differences, yielding a more robust edge map.  
• Better recovers fine detail in high-frequency regions without “flooding” uniform areas.

Cons:  
• Requires additional shifts (and possibly larger kernel sizes for diagonals) to avoid ghosting.  
• May generate additional artifacts if the underlying image contains noise or soft gradients.

─────────────────────────────  
Approach 3: Multi-Scale Difference-of-Gaussian (DoG) Edge Detection  
─────────────────────────────  
Description:  
Incorporate scale by comparing a minimally blurred image to one with a stronger Gaussian blur. This multi-scale approach, known as Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG), targets both subtle and pronounced edges. It works on combined image passes (diffuse, albedo, light) and can be tuned for sensitivity to texture versus sharp shadows.

Math Formulation:  
Let G(σ, I) denote a Gaussian blur on image I with standard deviation σ. Then:  

  Edge = |G(σ₁, I) − G(σ₂, I)|, with σ₂ > σ₁  

Optionally, a power transform may be applied:  

  Edge_out = (Edge)^α, then clamped to [0,1].

Pseudocode:  
--------------------------------------------------------  
G1 = GaussianBlur(I, sigma1)  
G2 = GaussianBlur(I, sigma2) // sigma2 > sigma1  
for each pixel (x, y):  
  diff = abs(G1(x, y) - G2(x, y))  
  edge = clamp(diff^α, 0, 1)  
  store edge at (x, y)  
--------------------------------------------------------  

Pros:  
• Flexibility in capturing both broad and fine details by adjusting σ₁, σ₂, and α.  
• Helps reduce spurious noise by leveraging the smoothing effect in the larger-scale blur.

Cons:  
• More computationally intensive (more blur passes, added parameter tuning).  
• May require careful calibration to ensure edges are not “washed out” or overly thick, especially in textured areas.

─────────────────────────────  
Approach 4: Hybrid Edge Mix (Normal + Diffuse) with Conditional Weighting  
─────────────────────────────  
Description:  
Fuse edge information derived separately from the normal pass and the combined (diffuse/albedo/light) pass. With conditional weighting, you can favor one domain (geometry vs. color/light contrasts) in different regions. For instance, the algorithm can use the normal-based edge detection for distinct geometry boundaries while falling back on the color-based DoG for texture details.

Math Formulation:  
Let:  

  E_normal = edge from enhanced normal pass  
  E_color  = edge from combined pass (e.g., DoG or Laplacian)  

Then mix them using a weight mask W that can be based on local variance or a preset threshold:  

  E_final = W · E_normal + (1 − W) · E_color  

For instance, W may be defined as:  

  W = step( variance_norm - V_threshold )  

or a smooth transition using a logistic function.

Pseudocode:  
--------------------------------------------------------  
for each pixel (x, y):  
  e_norm = ComputeNormalEdge(n(x,y), b, T, S)  
  e_color = ComputeCombinedEdge(I, x, y) // e.g., via Laplacian or DoG  
  W = ComputeWeight(variance(x, y), V_threshold) // returns value in [0,1]  
  E_final = clamp( W * e_norm + (1 - W) * e_color, 0, 1 )  
  store E_final at (x, y)  
--------------------------------------------------------  

Pros:  
• Offers the most flexibility by treating geometry and color/light details separately.  
• Detail separation enables non-uniform “line art” effects – for example, using strong normals for crisp boundaries and softer edges for painted or textured areas.

Cons:  
• Requires calibration of an additional weighting function and possibly more complex node arrangements.  
• Increases compositing complexity and may slow down processing if multiple passes are computed simultaneously.

─────────────────────────────  
Summary  
─────────────────────────────  
• Approach 1 refines your current normal-pass “dot product” method by adding adaptive clamping so you can keep subtle details without manual masking.  
• Approach 2 replaces simple subtraction with a Laplacian to capture multi-directional gradients in the combined pass.  
• Approach 3 introduces a multi-scale Difference-of-Gaussians method to allow detail capture at varying scales.  
• Approach 4 offers a hybrid solution that conditionally mixes geometry-based and color/light-based edges to tailor the final line art for different materials and lighting situations.

Each approach comes with its trade-offs; the best solution might even combine parts of more than one method, depending on the artistic look desired in your 3D render outlines—all achievable within Blender’s compositor using carefully built node networks.

    };

```cpp
    size_t size = 0;

    void push_front(T val) {
        auto newNode = std::make_unique<Node>(std::move(val));
        newNode->next = std::move(head);
        head = std::move(newNode);
        size++;
    }

    // Remove from front of list
    void pop_front() {
        if (!head) return;
        head = std::move(head->next);
        size--;
    }

    // Remove first occurrence of value
    void remove(const T& value) {
        if (!head) return;

        if (head->data == value) {
            pop_front();
            return;
        }

        Node* current = head.get();
        while (current->next) {
            if (current->next->data == value) {
                current->next = std::move(current->next->next);
                size--;
                return;
            }
            current = current->next.get();
        }
    }

    // Automatic memory management is handled by unique_ptr destructors
    ~LinkedList() = default;

    // Print list contents
    void print() const {
        Node* current = head.get();
        while (current) {
            std::cout << current->data << " ";
            current = current->next.get();
        }
        std::cout << "\n";
    }

    size_t getSize() const { return size; }
};

        tempList.push_front(42);
        tempList.push_front(99);
        std::cout << "Temporary list: ";
        tempList.print(); // 99 42
    } // Automatically destroyed here
    
    list.push_front(10);
    std::cout << "Final list: ";
    list.print(); // 10 3
```
